c.tagline: The first city of the Americas — cobblestone Zona Colonial, a Caribbean Malecón, and merengue.

taxi.fareNote: Street taxis are unmetered — agree the fare before getting in. App-based Uber and InDrive are widely used, cheaper, and give an upfront price; motoconcho (motorbike) taxis are common for short hops.

emergency.note: 911 is the unified national emergency line for police, fire, and ambulance across the Dominican Republic.

hood_landmark.Malecón / Bella Vista: Malecon Santo Domingo George Washington Avenue
hood_landmark.Zona Colonial: Zona Colonial Santo Domingo Calle Las Damas

avoid.reason: Caution in Cristo Rey, Capotillo and the colonial-zone fringes at night; petty crime/scams

hood_desc: The oldest European-founded city in the Americas and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, a walkable grid of cobblestone streets around Calle El Conde and Parque Colón, home to the first cathedral of the New World, the Alcázar de Colón, and Calle Las Damas; the atmospheric first-timer base packed with cafes, bars, and colonial museums.

A leafy, centrally located older neighborhood of tree-lined streets and early-20th-century homes between the Colonial Zone and the Malecón, home to the National Palace, the Plaza de la Cultura museums, and the Palacio de Bellas Artes; quiet, cultural, and budget-friendly.

An upscale, modern district of glass high-rises, luxury hotels, fine dining, and designer shopping (Blue Mall and Ágora Mall nearby); the polished business-and-nightlife heart of the modern city, safe and walkable in parts.
An affluent, lively neighborhood next to Piantini filled with restaurants, rooftop bars, cafes, and shopping malls; a favorite for a dressier night out and modern comforts away from the tourist core.

The Caribbean waterfront along Avenida George Washington, a palm-lined boulevard of big hotels, casinos, monuments, and weekend open-air merengue; lively and scenic, though some stretches feel run-down, so stick to the hotel corridor.

water.note: Drink bottled water; even locals avoid the tap.

transit.hours: The Metro runs roughly 6:00 AM to 10:30 PM (extended on weekends), and the Teleférico keeps similar hours. Guaguas run all day but thin out after dark, so most visitors switch to Uber or InDrive at night.
transit.note: The two-line Metro and the Teleférico cable car are clean, cheap, and safe but don't reach the Colonial Zone or the Malecón directly; within the walkable Zona Colonial you go on foot, and Uber/InDrive fill the gaps.
transit.pay: The Metro and Teleférico share the rechargeable Tarjeta metro card, tapped at turnstiles; a single ride is about RD$20. OMSA buses take cash, and informal guaguas are paid in cash to the cobrador (roughly RD$25-40). Uber and InDrive charge in-app by cash or card.

tip.r: Restaurants add a 10% service charge plus 18% ITBIS tax; leaving an extra 5-10% for good service is customary. Round up for taxis.

landmarks: Zona Colonial
The first European city of the Americas, a UNESCO grid of cobbled streets, ochre mansions and firsts — first cathedral, hospital and university.
Catedral Primada de América
Completed in 1540, the New World's first cathedral blends Gothic vaults with a golden coral-limestone Plateresque facade on Parque Colón.
Alcázar de Colón
The 1510s palace of Diego Columbus, son of the explorer, overlooks Plaza de España with the Caribbean's finest colonial-era furnishings.
Fortaleza Ozama
The oldest European military fort in the Americas, its 1502 Torre del Homenaje still glowering over the mouth of the Ozama River.
Calle de las Damas
The New World's first paved street, a stately promenade of colonial palaces, the Panteón Nacional and a 1753 sundial.
Los Tres Ojos
Three jewel-toned underground lakes glimmer in an open limestone cavern reached by stone steps and a hand-pulled raft.
Faro a Colón (Columbus Lighthouse)
A colossal cross-shaped 1992 monument said to hold Columbus's remains, projecting a crucifix of light into the Caribbean night sky.
Museo de las Casas Reales
The Spanish crown's colonial governance palace now chronicles conquest, piracy and trade with armour, galleon treasure and period rooms.
Monasterio de San Francisco
The romantically ruined first monastery of the New World becomes the backdrop for beloved open-air son and merengue dance nights.
Malecón de Santo Domingo
The palm-lined seafront boulevard stretches for kilometres along the Caribbean, ideal for sunset strolls past monuments and merengue bars.

train.note: There is no intercity or international passenger railway in the Dominican Republic - the old sugar-estate and Ferrocarril Central lines stopped carrying passengers decades ago and nothing crosses to Haiti by rail. What Santo Domingo does have is the Caribbean's most extensive urban rail: two OPRET metro lines through the capital, complemented by the Teleferico cable car to Los Alcarrizos and the Santo Domingo monorail projects. These cover the city well but stop at the city limits, so intercity travel is by coach. Metro fares use a rechargeable Tarjeta Ticket bought at station machines.

bus.note: Caribe Tours and Metro Servicios Turísticos run comfortable intercity coaches across the Dominican Republic (Santiago, Puerto Plata, Punta Cana) and cross-border services to Haiti — carry your passport for the border.

intl.to: San Juan (Puerto Rico) - sails from the Don Diego terminal on the Ozama river beside the Zona Colonial, ~12 hr overnight

ferry.note: Ferries del Caribe runs the overnight car-and-passenger ferry between Santo Domingo and San Juan, Puerto Rico, from the Don Diego terminal a short walk from the Zona Colonial; sailings are a few times a week and take roughly twelve hours, with cabins rather than seats. The service has been suspended and restored more than once in recent years, so confirm it is selling before building an itinerary around it. Vehicles must be booked ahead and you need the same documents as for a flight to Puerto Rico, including a US visa or ESTA where applicable. There are no other international ferry links.
